articles.title: A Maharashtra farmer's daughter who battled iron deficiency went on to make bajra flour last six months instead of 10 days; her millet initiative now reaches over 4 lakh children and earned a TIME100 Next India spot
articles.summary: A personal struggle with iron deficiency led a young food technologist to rethink an everyday grain.
articles.body: A personal struggle with iron deficiency led a young food technologist to rethink an everyday grain. Today, her innovation is helping take millet-based nutrition to schoolchildren across rural India, earning her a place on TIME100 Next India 2026.When Vidhya Parshuramkar struggled with iron deficiency, she did not imagine that the experience would eventually lead her to work on a solution for thousands of children. But the health challenge made her question something bigger: if she, despite having access to education and information, could struggle with proper nutrition, how many children in rural India were facing the same problem without even knowing it? The answer became the starting point of her journey.A farmer’s daughter from Maharashtra, Vidhya chose to look at a grain that had long been part of India's food culture but was gradually losing space in modern diets: pearl millet, or bajra. What followed was a food-processing innovation, a rural nutrition initiative and a growing effort to make nutritious food accessible to children. Her work has now earned her a place on the TIME100 Next India 2026 list, recognising emerging changemakers whose work is shaping the country's future.When a personal health struggle became a purposeVidhya's interest in nutrition was rooted in her own experience of anaemia. While pursuing her master's degree in food technology at IIT Kharagpur, she began exploring the nutritional value of millets, particularly pearl millet, which is naturally rich in iron. But she soon realised that knowing which food was nutritious was only part of the problem. Making it accessible, affordable, easy to store and suitable for large-scale distribution was another challenge altogether.Bajra has long been consumed in Indian households, especially in rural communities. However, once ground into flour, it tends to spoil quickly. Its short shelf life makes it difficult for manufacturers to store it for long periods, transport it across locations and turn it into products that can reach more people. Vidhya decided to tackle this problem through food science rather than leave the grain's nutritional potential untapped. Her journey eventually took her from working as an intern at Agrozee Organics to becoming a co-founder, where she began developing solutions that could connect nutrition, technology and rural livelihoods.The breakthrough that made bajra last six monthsThe biggest hurdle was the grain's shelf life. Bajra flour typically stays fresh for only about 10 to 15 days before its quality begins to deteriorate. This happens because of lipase, an enzyme that contributes to rancidity after milling. Vidhya developed a food-processing innovation known as Hydro-NIR technology, which deactivates the enzyme responsible for the deterioration. The process extends the shelf life of pearl millet flour from around 10 days to six months, without preservatives or compromising its iron content.The breakthrough made it easier to store, process and distribute millet-based food products over longer periods. It also opened the door to creating convenient nutrition products that could reach children in schools and communities where access to diverse food options remains a challenge.Instead of keeping the innovation confined to research, Vidhya helped translate it into products people could actually consume. Her work became the foundation of Agrozee Organics' millet-focused initiative, Millets Now, which aims to bring traditional grains back into everyday diets through practical food solutions.From a small initiative to 4 lakh childrenOne of the most meaningful parts of Vidhya's work is Nutri Dabba, a programme designed to improve children's access to millet-based nutrition. Through the initiative, schoolchildren receive millet-based food products such as cookies, laddoos, bars and other nutritious snacks. The idea is to make nutrition easier to incorporate into children's daily routines, rather than relying only on awareness about healthy eating.What began on a smaller scale has reportedly grown to reach more than 4 lakh schoolchildren, particularly in rural communities. The programme also aims to address iron deficiency and encourage children to develop healthier eating habits from an early age.The initiative works with rural women through self-help groups, creating opportunities for them to participate in making and distributing the products. This means the effort is not only about putting nutritious food into children's hands but also about creating livelihoods within the communities it serves. The model also connects the work to farmers. Agrozee Organics works with thousands of smallholder farmers, helping build demand for traditional crops such as pearl millet and creating a market for their produce.Recognition for a mission rooted in rural IndiaBefore her TIME recognition, Vidhya received the Rohini Nayyar Prize 2025, becoming its youngest recipient at the age of 24 and the first woman to receive the award. The honour recognised her contribution to rural development through nutrition, food innovation and women's empowerment. Her work is also creating opportunities beyond food distribution. Through Agrozee Organics, she has been associated with thousands of farmers and rural women, helping build a model that connects agriculture, food processing and community livelihoods.For Vidhya, the journey is deeply personal. She grew up in a farming family, experienced nutritional deficiency herself, and went on to use her education to find a solution rooted in an ingredient familiar to millions of Indian households. Her story is a reminder that sometimes, meaningful change does not begin with inventing something entirely new. It begins with looking at what already exists, understanding why it is not reaching people, and finding a way to make it work better.By giving bajra flour a longer shelf life and taking millet-based nutrition to children, Vidhya is turning a traditional grain into an opportunity for healthier communities. Her recognition on TIME100 Next India is not just about a food technology breakthrough but about an idea that could make nutrition, livelihoods and rural innovation grow together.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kiss cam CEO Andy Byron returns to tech with new job at Materialize after Coldplay scandal
articles.summary: Andy Byron returns to the tech industry as Chief Revenue Officer of Materialize after his controversial kiss cam incident at a Coldplay concert. Discover details on his new advisory position and the fallout from the scandal.
articles.body: Former Astronomer chief executive Andy Byron has returned to the technology industry, taking up a senior position at software startup Materialize more than a year after his appearance on a Coldplay concert's kiss cam led to his departure from the company.Byron joined the database company earlier this month as its chief revenue officer, according to TMZ. However, he has described his involvement as an advisory position rather than a full-time executive appointment.Materialize CEO Nate Stewart confirmed the hiring, saying the company had brought Byron on board to support its expansion plans.“We’re growing quickly and brought Andy on as a fractional CRO to support us as we scale,” Stewart told TMZ.Byron also addressed his new position, telling the outlet: “I’m just helping out as an advisor.”He added that he was advising several companies but did not hold a full-time position at any of them.Materialize, which has around 50 employees, appointed Byron with the support of Stewart and its board, TMZ reported. Staff was informed of his arrival during an organisation-wide meeting on November 11, two days after he began working with the company.Byron's return to the corporate sector comes after the controversy surrounding his appearance at Coldplay's concert at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, on July 16 last year.He was attending the performance alongside Kristin Cabot, who was then Astronomer's chief people officer, when the pair appeared on the stadium's kiss cam. Footage showed Cabot turning away from the camera while Byron moved out of its view after they appeared together on the big screen.Coldplay frontman Chris Martin made a remark about the reaction, while footage of the incident quickly circulated online. The clip also triggered widespread speculation about the relationship between the two executives, both of whom were married at the time.Astronomer's board subsequently launched an investigation into the incident. Byron resigned as chief executive on July 19, three days after the concert, while Cabot left the company several days later.Byron had led the data technology company since 2023 but largely stayed out of public view following his departure.Cabot later addressed the incident in an interview with The New York Times in December 2025, saying she and Byron had not been dating and describing their conduct at the concert as an alcohol-fuelled mistake. She also said the two had little communication afterwards.In March this year, Cabot discussed the episode further during an appearance on The Oprah Podcast. She revealed that her estranged husband, Andrew Cabot, had also attended the concert that evening.During the conversation with Oprah Winfrey, Cabot suggested that Byron had not been truthful with her about the status of his marriage. She said she believed he was in the process of separating from his wife when they attended the concert.“He wasn’t the person he represented himself to be, to me — and lying is a non-negotiable for me,” Cabot told Winfrey.She also said she had stopped communicating with Byron the previous autumn. Cabot declined to provide further details about the alleged misrepresentation, saying she did not want to involve his family in the controversy.Byron has not publicly addressed the circumstances surrounding the concert incident or his departure from Astronomer.You use AI every day. articles.title: Shropshire landowners create wetlands to help reduce River Severn flooding
articles.summary: Landowners are helping create wetlands, ponds and leaky dams as part of efforts to slow water flow.
articles.body:
Tiny wetlands scattered across the Shropshire countryside are playing a growing role in the fight against flooding, with landowners helping to slow rainwater before it reaches the River Severn.

Communities across Shropshire and Worcestershire have repeatedly seen homes flooded, roads closed and flood barriers deployed when the river bursts its banks after periods of heavy rain.

Now, landowners are backing a programme of wetlands, ponds and "leaky dams" designed to hold water higher up the catchment and reduce pressure on towns and villages further downstream.

A project in the Gatton Valley, Shropshire, has already led to the creation of about 60 wetlands aimed at storing rainwater before it reaches rivers and streams feeding into the Severn.

The work forms part of the Severn Valley Water Management Scheme's Rea Brook project, funded by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) and managed by Shropshire Council.

The scheme is testing ways of slowing the flow of water through the landscape, reducing both the speed and volume of water reaching more populated areas.

While a single wetland may only hold back a relatively small amount of water, experts say the combined effect of dozens of schemes across a catchment can make a meaningful difference to flood management.

Among those taking part are landowners Matt and Drew, who have helped create six wetlands, 12 leaky dams and drainage features on their land.

The measures divert rainwater from roads and fields into areas where it can be stored temporarily before gradually draining away.

One of the leaky dams creates a pool during heavy rain, allowing water to collect before slowly seeping through, rather than rushing downstream all at once.

Drew said the changes had "dried out the ground a little bit" by holding water "in one spot".

"We're doing our little bit to contribute to holding back the water from flooding further downstream," he said.

The work has also brought environmental benefits. Matt said the wetlands have attracted wildlife including dragonflies, frogs, toads and newts.

Cecilia Young, catchment officer at Severn Rivers Trust, said keeping water off roads was especially important in more remote parts of the valley, where flooding could leave communities cut off.

"The work we've done here and the adjacent farm has been trying to target keeping water off the little minor roads, which are really essential for people up here during a flood," she said.

She said the contribution made by individual landowners might appear modest in isolation, but became far more significant when repeated across an entire river catchment.

"It maybe feels like there's not a lot of water being held back. Sometimes we feel like it's a couple of bathtubs worth, which doesn't make much difference when you're flooding Shrewsbury," she said.

"But every little wetland is contributing to a much bigger picture."

The Gatton Valley project is one of several helping to shape a long-term strategy for managing flood risk across the upper Severn catchment.

Alongside wetlands and leaky dams, organisations involved in the scheme are exploring tree planting, changes to land management and traditional flood defences as communities across Shropshire and Worcestershire continue to face the threat of flooding.

Tom Dainty, deputy cabinet member with responsibility for flooding at Shropshire Council, said: "Flood risk is not something we can tackle with one solution in one place.

"Projects like this show the value of working with landowners and partners across the catchment to slow water down and manage it closer to where it falls.

"Each intervention may be relatively small but together they can make our communities and local infrastructure more resilient."

articles.title: Russian ‘triple-tap’ attack in Ukraine kills emergency worker and 7-year-old in Zelensky’s home city
articles.summary: A seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic were killed Friday night in a Russian “triple-tap” strike on the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, according to local authorities.
articles.body: A seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic were killed Friday night in a Russian “triple-tap” strike on the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, according to local authorities. In the attack on the home city of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, ballistic missiles hit a restaurant parking lot, then jet-powered drones struck rescue workers responding, city mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said. A further drone strike hit the location for a short time later. This latest Russian assault comes after a busy week of diplomacy, including an unprecedented meeting between US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Trump described Putin as a “friend” when they met – but in a CNN interview after, Zelensky said “for us, he is a killer.” Nearly 60 others including rescuers and police officers were injured in the initial strike and follow-up attacks, Vilkul said. He described the events as a “tragic evening and a tragic night for our city,” adding that the attack occurred “in the city center, near a popular restaurant, on Children’s Day.” In Ukraine, Children’s Day falls on November 20 and serves as a reminder of the need to protect children’s rights and advocate for their safety. Dramatic footage from authorities showed people moving away from debris strewn across the street, only to scramble for cover as the sound of another incoming strike rings out. Of those wounded, 28 remain hospitalized including children, among them a three-year-old girl, as well as five people in intensive care. “Doctors are doing everything necessary to save their lives. Our condolences go out to the families and loved ones of those who died… We pray for the swiftest possible recovery of the injured,” the mayor said. Local broadcasting outlet Rudana named the seven-year-old boy who was killed in the Russian attack as Tikhon, describing him as kind, quick-witted and talented. The boy’s family did not live in Kryvyi Rih, which is Zelensky’s hometown, but had been in the central Ukrainian city on business and decided to stop by their favourite restaurant, the outlet reported. “We didn’t live here because it’s dangerous… but danger caught up with us,” the boy’s mother, Olena, told the outlet. According to the report, two of Olena’s other sons are in intensive care following the strike. Zelensky said the attack on Friday night hit an ordinary civilian area of the city. “There are no military facilities nearby, and there never have been,” he said. “Cities and villages in the Kharkiv, Donetsk, Dnipro, Rivne, Chernihiv, Mykolaiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions were also hit. In the Sumy region, a railway station came under attack,” the Ukrainian leader added. Trump held talks with Putin and Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, a meeting which was followed by a large “Coalition of the Willing” gathering in Berlin, attended by European leaders as well as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. In a joint statement after the meeting, the group of key Ukrainian allies declared they were ready to join direct negotiations with Moscow, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Russia’s “maximalist demands are not realistic.” Zelensky on Saturday described the three-way meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi as “very unsuccessful” for the Russian leader, who he said had failed in his goal of trying to recreate a Yalta-style conference at which Allied powers divided up the postwar world in 1945. “China did not let itself be drawn in. As for the United States, I don’t know what went on between them and Russia in their bilateral talks, but Ukraine was not discussed. Nothing was said publicly,” Zelensky said in audio messages shared with journalists. “So, the plan to redraw the world’s borders didn’t work out… I think the summit was a major failure for Russia.”

articles.title: FBI Ten Most Wanted cartel leader 'Chapo Isidro' captured by Mexico's 'elite military forces' after US help
articles.summary: FBI Ten Most Wanted fugitive Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, who goes by the alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured in Guasave, Mexico, sparking a gun battle.
articles.body: One of the FBI's Ten Most Wanted fugitives has been captured in Mexico following a joint U.S.-Mexico operation where the arresting force "came under attack with gunfire and explosives," authorities announced Saturday. Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, described by the FBI as the "alleged leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, a heavily armed, major drug-trafficking organization based in Sinaloa, Mexico," was detained in the city of Guasave. The State Department previously issued a $5 million reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of Meza-Flores, who went by the alias "Chapo Isidro." Mexico's Secretariat of National Defense said Meza-Flores was detained during a military raid carried out by the special forces personnel. U.S. and Mexican intelligence agencies coordinated in the lead-up to the operation, which also netted the arrests of the cartel's second in command and a financial operator. "The operation to carry out these arrests was conducted by elite military forces, which, after precisely locating the target using various technological tools, carried it out in three phases, as follows," the Secretariat of National Defense wrote on X. "Arrival in the target area: this was carried out using stealth and surprise via different land access routes to the arrest area. ALLEGED JALISCO CARTEL LEADER ACCUSED OF DRUG TRAFFICKING AND FUEL SMUGGLING ARRESTED IN MEXICO "Establishing security and capturing the target: this was carried out near the detainees’ location by setting up an internal and external security perimeter to prevent escape or the arrival of reinforcements," it continued. "The arresting force came under attack with gunfire and explosives, prompting it to enter the house to capture the individuals in question. "Evacuation of the target: after the detainees’ identities were confirmed, they were evacuated to Mexico City aboard a Mexican Air Force aircraft to be placed at the disposal of the competent prosecutorial authorities," it also said. Video released by the Secretariat of National Defense showed Mexican military personnel moving a handcuffed suspect into a truck. KASH PATEL DEFENDS FBI'S ‘MOST WANTED’ BUSTS AMID MANIPULATION ACCUSATIONS, HIGHLIGHTS 'SUMMER HEAT' SUCCESS In its Ten Most Wanted Fugitive poster, the FBI said Meza-Flores "is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation, and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico." "Meza-Flores was originally indicted on May 2, 2012, in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia. On November 26, 2019, a federal superseding indictment and federal arrest warrant were issued for Meza-Flores in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia after he was charged with multiple counts of Drug-Trafficking Violations and Use and Possession of a Firearm," it added. The operation surrounding Meza-Flores' arrest forced the cancellation of a Mexican Pacific League baseball game in progress in Guasave on Friday, with video on social media purportedly showing players and fans running for safety at Kuroda Park while gunfire rang out in the background. articles.title: 11 killed in burst of violence in northern Mexico after capture of cartel leader
articles.summary: GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — A burst of violence in Mexico’s Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isi...
articles.body:
GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — A burst of violence in Mexico's Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," left at least 11 people dead, authorities said Saturday.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after an intense firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized and trucks and businesses burning.

Mexico's Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.

The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.

As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.

Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violence

The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city.

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

"The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city."

Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him.

Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities.

Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case.

"Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.

Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.

"Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.

An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation.

Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday.

"The aftermath of last night's war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down," Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico.

Guasave residents remained "very afraid" because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said.

Capture prompts celebration and warnings

Meza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.

"Results like these don't happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together," U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. "We will continue the hunt."

Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins , including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes , known as " El Mencho ," who was killed by the military in February.

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.

The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

Janetsky and Sánchez reported from Mexico City. Associated Press writer Thomas Strong contributed to this report from Washington.

articles.title: Princess Kate reflects on life after cancer diagnosis in a new documentary
articles.summary: Britain’s Catherine, Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.
articles.body: LONDON — Britain’s Catherine, Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024. “Heal” follows 44-year-old Kate as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. She completed the feat in June to raise money for the cancer charity of the Royal Marsden Hospital, where she was treated. In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Kate’s Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences. Kate, who is married to the heir to the British throne, announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for. Kate disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month. In the trailer, Kate says cancer changes people profoundly, and “healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.” She adds that “it’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone” and “often, it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.” Kensington Palace said proceeds from its distribution will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity. In the United States, the documentary will air on NBC on Monday, 30 November, streaming on Peacock from Tuesday, 1 December.

articles.title: French police officers convicted of racist assault on Black music producer
articles.summary: The lawyer for a Black man who was beaten up by three French police officers hailed a “historic ruling” on Saturday after a court acknowledged the racist nature of the violence and sentenced them to between one and two years in prison.
articles.body: The lawyer for a Black man who was beaten up by three French police officers hailed a “historic ruling” on Saturday after a court acknowledged the racist nature of the violence and sentenced them to between one and two years in prison. The assault on Michel Zecler, a music producer, took place six years ago during the coronavirus pandemic and was caught on camera. It showed the officers repeatedly punching him, using a truncheon and tear gas against him for no apparent reason. Zecler told The Associated Press after the incident that the officers hurled repeated insults at him, including a very strong racist epithet. “What is very important is that the racist nature of the violence he suffered has been recognized,” Zecler’s lawyer, Serge Money, told France Info. “As a legal professional, one can only be satisfied. This is a first.” Money said that from the very beginning of the proceedings, Zecler maintained that he had been racially insulted, whereas the defendants’ accounts were somewhat inconsistent. “Ultimately, they were convicted of lying, as the falsification of written records was established,” he said. The verdict was issued late Friday in Paris. Videos published showed the violent arrest of Zecler in the 17th arrondissement of the French capital. The three officers intended to stop him for not wearing a face mask during the restrictions imposed because of the pandemic. The video images, obtained by the AP, both from a security camera inside the studio and filmed by neighbors outside, showed officers following Zecler inside his music studio, where they could be seen repeatedly punching him and beating him with a truncheon. “I want to understand why I have been assaulted by people who were wearing a police uniform,” Zecler told AP at the time. “I want justice actually, because I believe in the justice of my country.” Zecler suffered injuries to his head, forearms and legs. French law enforcement agencies have long faced complaints of excessive force. After Zecler was taken into custody for violence against public authority, then-Justice Minister Eric Dupond-Moretti said in a television interview that he was scandalized by the images. He admitted that some officers were racists, but denied systemic racism within the force. Money said that without the video, Zecler would have ended up in prison. He added that the officers apologized. “This ruling should set a precedent for all those who have not been believed,” he said. “There has to be a first, a starting point. It is now up to the justice system to make use of this ruling. I have no doubt that everyone will recognize its significance. This is no small matter, particularly given that the investigating judges had initially dismissed the racist dimension of the case.” Rap artist Stomy Bugsy said “this is a victory for all victims. If it can help curb, reduce and ultimately put an end to this kind of police misconduct and abuse, then it is a victory.”

On November 21, 2020, Michel Zecler was the victim of a violent beating at the hands of police officers, captured by surveillance cameras. Six years after - and with the trial of the police officers approaching on November 9 - the music producer remains deeply affected, both emotionally and by a sense of "anger" regarding the police violence that he believes continues to persist in France.

articles.title: 11 killed in burst of violence in northern Mexico after capture of cartel leader
articles.summary: Mexican authorities captured top cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” in the Mexican state of Sinaloa overnight, resulting in a burst of violence that rattled civilians.
articles.body: A burst of violence in Mexico’s Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” left at least 11 people dead, authorities said Saturday. Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after a heavy firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized and trucks and businesses burning. Mexico’s Defense Cabinet on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed. The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms. Mexico’s government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores. He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos,” a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state. Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico’s government to go after criminal groups. As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warn that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions. Mexican forces’ move against cartel fuels violence The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead and opened fire on key locations across the city. Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders. “The fighting was happening all over Guasave,” said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. “It spread throughout the city.” Mexican authorities said that they used “stealth and surprise” to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. He was later taken by aircraft to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors. Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage escorting a man through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck. No casualties have been reported so far as a result of the operation. Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to discuss the case. “Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary,” the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least “10 roadblocks” with burning vehicles on Guasave’s streets. Terror in Sinaloa Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations. “Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks,” Sánchez told The Associated Press. She said that the city’s firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning. An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. Authorities didn’t provide details on how many people were wounded or killed in the clashes. Burned out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday. “The aftermath of last night’s war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down,” Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico. Guasave residents remained “very afraid” because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said. Capture prompts celebration and warnings Meza Flores’ detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office. The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities. “Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together,” U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. “We will continue the hunt.” Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention “an important step in pacifying Sinaloa.” Sheinbaum’s government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as “ El Mencho,” who was killed by the military in February. Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run. The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa. “What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States,” Saucedo said. “What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don’t dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact.”

articles.title: 'Working to suppress India’s rise': US panel report flags China's support to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor
articles.summary: China’s military support to Pakistan during the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict added to New Delhi’s security challenges and raised concerns about a
articles.body: China’s military support to Pakistan during the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict added to New Delhi’s security challenges and raised concerns about a possible two-front threat, a US congressional commission report has said. The report said Beijing has been working across military, economic and maritime domains to constrain India’s rise as a strategic power.The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, in its report on China’s efforts to expand global power and influence, said the conflict following Operation Sindoor highlighted how Beijing could strengthen Pakistan during a crisis without directly entering the fighting.According to the report, Pakistan used advanced weaponry procured from China during the fighting. It also said China reportedly increased pressure on India by deploying a survey vessel with advanced sensors around waters within India's exclusive economic zone (EEZ) as tensions escalated.The report further noted that military officials in India had claimed after the conflict that Pakistan may have received real-time satellite imagery or other intelligence support from Beijing. China neither confirmed nor overtly denied the claim, it said.In May 2026, China's state-run CCTV aired an interview with Zhang Heng, an engineer from the Aviation Industry Corporation (AVIC) of China's Chengdu Aircraft Design and Research Institute, a key developer of fighter aircraft and uncrewed autonomous vehicles. Zhang confirmed that he and other Chinese AVIC personnel provided onsite technical support in Pakistan during the May 2025 conflict, the report said.What report said on China suppressing India's riseThe report said India’s size, military strength and strategic location make it a significant factor in the long-term competition with China. It noted that India is the world’s most populous country and largest democracy, and shares a 2,100-mile contested border with China. Its position along key sea lanes in the Indian Ocean also gives it strategic importance.“China understands this, and it is actively working to suppress India’s rise across multiple domains,” the report said.It said Beijing was continuing its military buildup, asserting sovereignty claims along the disputed border, deepening military support for Pakistan and expanding its naval and surveillance presence in the Indian Ocean.The report described China's economic leverage as its “sharpest tool”. It said Beijing was “using its control over critical industrial inputs, technology, and expertise to preserve its manufacturing advantages and make it harder for India to build competing capacity”.Citing examples, the report said China had “restricted exports of key inputs and products to India to exert economic pressure”, “recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India’s electronics manufacturing”, and “slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants”. It also said Beijing had imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry.The report further flagged China's move in 2025 to require Indian firms to certify that certain Chinese-supplied inputs would not be re-exported to the US. While Beijing suspended the requirement as part of the broader Trump-Xi trade détente, the report said it remained “a lever that can turn India’s dependence on China into a weapon aimed at U.S. supply chains”.China-Pakistan military partnershipThe report said China's growing military partnership with Pakistan has made the possibility of a two-front contingency an increasingly critical concern for India. Beijing has deepened its ties with Islamabad since the 1962 Sino-Indian war, with cooperation spanning defence, infrastructure and economic sectors."China’s evolving military partnership with Pakistan has made a two-front contingency an increasingly critical concern for India. The May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict demonstrated how China could strengthen Pakistan during a crisis without Beijing entering the fighting directly, adding to India’s concerns about how a future conflict with Pakistan could develop," it said.China is Pakistan's main defence supplier, accounting for 81% of its arms imports between 2020 and 2024, the report said.It added that China's military support to Pakistan has magnified the strategic challenges India faces in its longstanding rivalry with Islamabad, raising concerns that a conflict with one could escalate into a challenge involving both.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2025, a 24-year-old Montreal woman died mysteriously at an Istanbul hotel; food poisoning was suspected. A year later, investigation now points to deadly pesticide used to kill bedbugs
articles.summary: A 24-year-old Canadian woman who travelled to Turkey to celebrate her medical school graduation died suddenly in an Istanbul hotel, with a new
articles.body: A 24-year-old Canadian woman who travelled to Turkey to celebrate her medical school graduation died suddenly in an Istanbul hotel, with a new investigation raising questions about whether she was exposed to a highly toxic pesticide used to kill bedbugs. Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, from Montreal, died on June 17, 2025, after falling seriously ill during a holiday with friends. A Turkish autopsy attributed her death to food poisoning, but her family has challenged the findings, saying the explanation does not match the circumstances of her sudden deterioration.A joint investigation by CBC's The Fifth Estate and Radio-Canada's Enquête, published on November 20, 2026, has raised the possibility that she was exposed to phosphine gas, a deadly substance released by aluminium phosphide, a pesticide used to kill insects and rodents.The investigation also documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning in Turkey since 2023, including around 12 deaths.Bérengère had recently graduated from medical school and travelled to Turkey with a group of close friends to celebrate. After visiting Cappadocia, she and a friend headed to Istanbul for the final two days of their trip. The two women checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and spent the day sightseeing. They later ate a chicken casserole, followed by Turkish tea and baklava.The following morning, both woke up violently ill. Bérengère's travelling companion, identified by CBC under the pseudonym Laurie, said the young woman began vomiting within minutes of waking up. Laurie soon developed similar symptoms. The two women repeatedly rushed to the bathroom before realising that their condition was not improving. They contacted the hotel reception, and an ambulance took them to hospital.Back in Montreal, Bérengère's sister Éléonore received a FaceTime call from Laurie, who told her that they were in a hospital in Istanbul and that things were not looking good. Éléonore and her father, Henri Cattino, immediately began arranging flights to Turkey. While waiting for a connecting flight in Paris, she contacted the Canadian embassy to ask whether her sister had died. She was informed that Bérengère was dead.Family questions food poisoning diagnosisThe Turkish autopsy report, received by the family shortly before Christmas 2025, concluded that food poisoning had caused Bérengère's death. However, her relatives were unconvinced and asked Quebec authorities to examine the findings.Her sister said the Quebec coroner could not confirm food poisoning as the cause because there were no signs of intestinal irritation, which would typically be expected in such cases.A Quebec pathologist who reviewed the Turkish report also questioned the conclusion, pointing to how quickly Bérengère's condition had deteriorated.Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı, a professor emeritus and human rights activist, also reviewed the autopsy findings for the CBC investigation. "This is not food poisoning," she said, suggesting that pesticide exposure was a more likely explanation. She pointed to metabolic acidosis, a condition in which excessive acid builds up in the body, as a significant indicator of possible phosphine poisoning. Still, pesticide exposure has not been officially established as the cause of Bérengère's death.Hotel's neighbouring room had bedbug complaintsThe investigation uncovered a potentially significant detail about the hotel where the two women stayed. CBC journalists examined hundreds of online reviews of the Seven Days Hotel and found a complaint from a tourist who claimed he had suffered around 150 bedbug bites during his stay in June 2025.The man confirmed that he had occupied Room 107, immediately next to Room 108, where Bérengère and Laurie stayed around 10 days later. The windows of the two rooms opened towards each other. This raised questions about whether Room 107 had undergone chemical treatment to eliminate bedbugs before the women arrived.Hotel manager Bahattin Demir confirmed that the hotel regularly hired exterminators to spray its rooms. But he dismissed any link between the pesticide and the death. The pest control company, identified as Wolves, was also contacted by the journalists. During an undercover conversation, an employee described a treatment in which rooms had to remain sealed and unoccupied for 72 hours. The description resembled the use of aluminium phosphide, although the employee did not identify the chemical. When approached directly, the company denied using aluminium phosphide.The investigation also found that the women had initially kept their hotel window open but closed it the following evening and switched on the air conditioning. They became ill the next morning. Asked whether phosphine gas could accumulate in an air-conditioning system, forensic pathologist Fincancı said it was possible.Four-member family also died from phosphine poisoning in IstanbulBérengère's death came into focus again after another tragedy involving a family of four in Istanbul in November 2025. The Böcek family, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, fell ill during their stay in the city. All four members died within days. Investigators initially suspected food poisoning but determined that the family had been exposed to phosphine gas released during fumigation in a neighbouring hotel room. The pesticide involved was aluminium phosphide, which releases highly toxic phosphine gas when exposed to moisture. The chemical is used to kill rodents and insects, but its use in urban areas in Turkey is illegal. In June 2026, the owners of the extermination company involved in the Böcek family's deaths were sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received prison sentences ranging from 12 to 13 yearsCBC and Radio-Canada documented nearly 30 phosphine poisoning cases in Turkey since 2023, including approximately 12 deaths. Many of the victims were women and children, and several cases were initially suspected to be food poisoning.Canada issues travel warning over chemical poisoningIn September 2026, Canada updated its travel advisory for Turkey, warning travellers about cases of poisoning linked to chemical pesticides used in tourist accommodations in Istanbul. Following the broadcast of the CBC investigation on October 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted the broadcaster and confirmed that the investigation into Bérengère's death remained open, the CBC report said.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Cancer does change you’: Princess of Wales talks candidly about her experience in new documentary
articles.summary: Catherine, Princess of Wales is opening up about her experience with cancer in a deeply personal new documentary that offers a rare glimpse into the life of Britain’s future queen.
articles.body: Catherine, Princess of Wales is opening up about her experience with cancer in a deeply personal new documentary that offers a rare glimpse into the life of Britain’s future queen. “Cancer does change you. It changes your body. It changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you,” the 44-year-old says in a trailer for the film, “Heal.” The documentary, which premieres on the BBC on November 29, explores the emotional and physical toll of cancer and the challenges of recovery. “Often it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that,” Kate says in the trailer. The film follows the princess as she takes on the National Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. Hiking alongside her brother, James Middleton, Kate reveals she never rang a bell traditionally used to mark the end of cancer treatment. “I didn’t ring the bell,” she says. “Maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” James replies. The princess hopes the documentary will help others navigate diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer, while improving access to holistic cancer care that supports patients’ physical and emotional wellbeing, Kensington Palace said. Kate publicly revealed her cancer diagnosis in March 2024, two months after undergoing abdominal surgery. She announced that she had completed chemotherapy that September and confirmed in January 2025 that her cancer was in remission. She has not disclosed what type of cancer she had. All funds received through the documentary’s distribution have been directed to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, which supports the hospital where she was treated, to support people living with and beyond cancer, according to Kensington Palace. The princess has been slowly been returning to her royal work, accompanying her husband Prince William to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony earlier this week. The visit marked the couple’s first official overseas trip in four years and represented a major milestone in Kate’s return to duties since her cancer diagnosis. “Heal” will air in the United States on NBCUniversal on November 30, followed by Channel 9 in Australia on December 1 and CTV and Noovo in Canada on December 7.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills three in vehicle distributing aid in Gaza, witnesses say
articles.summary: Israeli forces hit a truck in Gaza on Saturday which witnesses said was carrying food and papers bearing the logo of the World Central Kitchen charity, but the organisation said the vehicle was not affiliated with it.
articles.body: Israeli forces hit a truck in Gaza on Saturday which witnesses said was carrying food and papers bearing the logo of the World Central Kitchen charity, but the organisation said the vehicle was not affiliated with it. The Gaza Health Ministry said three people were killed in the incident in Gaza City. The Israeli military said its forces had been targeting Islamic Jihad militants in the area at the time and that the vehicle had been transporting food to members of the organization. Reuters was unable to independently verify the Israeli military’s statement. Islamic Jihad did not immediately comment on the strike. World Central Kitchen said in a statement that the truck was unaffiliated with the charity, which distributes food in Gaza. It said a driver of the vehicle had previously worked for the charity and that the two others in the car were not WCK workers. After the strike, witnesses said they had discovered papers with the WCK logo on meals of cooked rice in the vehicle, Reuters video footage showed. Israel briefly launched a ground operation in Gaza earlier this week and killed six people in a strike on a hospital that it said was targeting a commander of the Palestinian militant group Hamas. An October 2025 US-backed ceasefire halted ​major fighting in the shattered territory but has not stopped ⁠Israeli attacks on Gaza or secured Hamas’ disarmament. At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since then, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies. Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along Gaza’s coast. Israel’s more than two-year-long assault on Gaza has killed tens of thousands, caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza’s entire population and led to assessments of genocide from scholars and a United Nations inquiry. Israel says its actions are self-defense after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than 250 hostages in an October 2023 attack on Israel.

articles.title: 'Goondaism isn't a bug': BJP, BRS attack Congress over Meta office vandalism
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP and BRS on Saturday accused the ruling Congress of damaging Hyderabad's business-friendly image after Youth Congress workers vandalised the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP and BRS on Saturday accused the ruling Congress of damaging Hyderabad's business-friendly image after Youth Congress workers vandalised the Meta office in the city on November 20, alleging that the incident had hurt 'Brand Hyderabad' and raised questions about the safety of companies operating in Telangana.The BJP and BRS leaders criticised the Congress over the incident, with both parties questioning the message it sent to businesses and investors.Responding to a post by the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) on X, which claimed that its "lions" had stormed the Meta office, Telangana BJP president N Ramchander Rao accused the Congress of encouraging disruptive behaviour."Goondaism isn't a bug" in Congress culture but a "feature", he said."Shameless? Nah. They’re FLEXING it because they know they’ll be rewarded," Rao said in a post on X.He alleged that Youth Congress workers had hijacked a plane in 1978 to demand Indira Gandhi's release and were later rewarded with Lok Sabha tickets.Referring to the recent protests at the AI Summit, Rao said Youth Congress workers had stormed the venue without clothes and attempted to ransack it in 2026. He also claimed that Congress leader Rahul Gandhi had hailed them as "Babbar Sher".Meanwhile, BRS working president K T Rama Rao said Hyderabad's reputation as a business destination had been built over decades through pro-business policies."Brand Hyderabad feeds millions of families across the country," he said."Congress goons thought vandalising Meta's office in Hyderabad was cool. These idiots are even bragging about it. In three years of your governance in Telangana, did you bring even ONE big brand like Meta to Hyderabad?" he said in a post on X.He also questioned Rahul Gandhi over the incident, asking whether goondaism was his way of bringing companies to India.Rama Rao pointed out that Meta has its largest campus in India in Hyderabad. He said the company chose the city because the government had assured it of a safe working environment."Yesterday's act didn't just break glass. It broke Brand Hyderabad's trust," he said.What happened at Meta officeYouth Congress workers, led by Telangana unit president Jakkidi Shiva Charan Reddy, vandalised the Meta office premises in Hyderabad on November 20. They damaged flowerpots during a protest against the social media company suspending the accounts of IYC national president Uday Bhanu Chib and other leaders.The protesters alleged that Meta was acting in favour of the BJP.Police took Shiva Charan Reddy and other Youth Congress workers into custody and shifted them to a police station, a Congress leader said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: After years of retail work, Sam Walton used $5,000 in savings and a $20,000 loan from his father-in-law to buy an Arkansas store in 1945; by its fifth year, it was recording annual sales of $250,000
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring journey of Sam Walton, who turned a failing retail store in Arkansas into the foundation for Walmart, revolutionizing discount retailing with innovative strategies and a commitment to customer value.
articles.body: A young retailer looking to start their first independent venture might have hoped for a better starting point. The shop on offer in Newport was losing money, and Sam Walton had little experience running an independent venture. Still, he took a chance on it anyway.American Business History recorded that on 1 September 1945, Walton bought the shop for $25,000. He used up $5,000 from his savings, and the rest, $20,000, he borrowed from his father-in-law, L.S. Robson. Fast forward to five years later, the languishing shop would see annual sales of $250,000 in a town of 7,000 people, the American Business History noted. Behind this boon were simple methods that Walton used: buy cheaply and sell at lower prices.Learning the ropes and a costly leaseWalton had worked as a management trainee at J.C. Penney in Des Moines before serving in the US military during the Second World War. At Penney’s he learnt the ins and outs of retailing and spent his lunch hours studying rival stores. Even during his military service, he continued reading about the trade and visited shops. When he returned to civilian life in 1945, he wanted a store of his own. Butler Brothers, the wholesaler who operated the Ben Franklin franchise system, offered him the Newport store.According to Harvard Business School, the purchase was riskier than Walton understood. He agreed to pay rent equivalent to 5% of sales, a figure exceptionally high for a variety store. The lease also lacked a renewal clause. Although Walton was inexperienced in running any kind of business, he did keep an eye on competitors, a skill he soon leveraged. The Sterling Store across the street was better managed, with more sales. Walton frequented the Sterling Store and checked its prices and displays. Butler Brothers provided him with training and an accounting system, while the rival shop showed what his store needed to improve.Breaking the supplier rulesWalton looked for merchandise beyond the suppliers approved by Butler Brothers. The franchise had mandated operators to buy at least 80% of their goods through the wholesaler. Walton, in a manner of speaking, went against the norm and sourced cheaper goods elsewhere, including shirts and underwear from Tennessee. He also used a New York broker who offered lower prices than Butler Brothers and reduced the selling prices. His decision to discount goods and make money through volumes of sales became a principle of Walmart. For instance, Walton sold four pairs of panties for a dollar while his competitors charged three for a dollar.Walton’s principle worked, and the store’s sales increased from $72,000 before Walton took over to $105,000 in his first year, then $140,000 the following year, to $175,000 in the third year, the Harvard Business School noted. Walton subsequently repaid Robson’s loan within two and a half years. By the fifth year, annual sales had reached $250,000, with a profit of between $30,000 and $40,000.Losing the lease and launching Walmart However, the business’s success did not secure its premises. When the lease expired, the landlord P.K. Holmes refused to renew the lease. He wanted to buy the store for his son. Because the agreement gave Walton no right to renew, he left Newport. Holmes purchased his inventory and fixtures for $50,000, according to Harvard Business School. He remained undaunted by loss, and said: “I’ve never been one to dwell on reverses, and I didn’t do so then”. According to American Business History, Walton then moved to Bentonville, Arkansas, and bought a dime store, which he reopened as Walton’s Five and Dime in July 1950, a precursor to Walmart. He remained a Ben Franklin franchisee but introduced self-service, with tills near the exit instead of clerks and registers throughout the shop. Sales rose exponentially from $32,000 to $95,000, American Business History noted. He then opened more stores in Arkansas and Missouri, with borrowed money to expand and oscillate frequently between locations.According to Harvard Business School, when Walton shifted to large-discount retailing near Rogers, Arkansas, he opened Walmart alongside Walton’s Five and Dime. Harvard Business School recorded that by 1969, Walmart had opened its 18th store in Newport, nineteen years after he had left.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2002, Richard Van Pham set out from Long Beach for a sail to Santa Catalina Island; nearly four months and 2,500 miles later, a US Navy frigate found him off Costa Rica
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable survival story of Richard Van Pham, who set sail from Long Beach and was rescued 2,500 miles away in Costa Rica after nearly four months at sea.
articles.body: Richard Van Pham was a retired furniture shop owner who left for a short sail. No search party was looking for him, and nobody reported him missing when he failed to return from a sailing trip off Southern California. The first sign that he was close to people came from an aircraft. After months of not seeing land or another vessel, he watched a plane pass overhead. By then he had drifted about 2,500 miles from Long Beach, and the Navy found him roughly 300 miles off Costa Rica.According to the Los Angeles Times, a storm broke the mast of his 26-foot sailboat named the Sea Breeze. The damage extended to its outboard motor and radio, thereby leaving him unable to call for help. He only went southward because of winds and ocean currents that carried his damaged sailboat.How he survived at seaPham packed enough food for a day trip. He collected rainwater in a five-gallon bucket and caught fish. To attract seabirds, he fastened some of the fish to the broken mast. Once caught, he cooked the birds on a makeshift grill made from the wood panelling removed from the boat. He also caught a sea turtle and salted its meat for later.Pham told the Los Angeles Times, “If you travel at sea, you take what you find. If you’re scared, you will die. During much of the day, he stayed below deck to avoid the sun. A solar-powered battery functioned from the sailboat, and he sometimes used it to watch videos on a small television. According to the Guardian on 26 September 2002, Pham had lost 40 pounds by the time he was found, although there were no obvious health problems.Rescued by the Navy and sinking the Sea BreezeAccording to the Los Angeles Times, finally, a U.S. Customs P-3 aircraft on a counter-narcotics patrol spotted the Sea Breeze and alerted the Navy. At the time, USS McClusky, a 453-foot frigate, was en route to completing a six-month patrol off Central America, and decided to probe further. Its crew saw the damaged sailboat and a man who was waving from the deck. They found Pham, who was delighted to see the sailors, preparing roasted seabirds for lunch.But instead of wanting medical treatment, he wanted help repairing the mast so he could continue sailing. Pham was under the impression that he was near Hawaii. Engineers aboard the frigate examined the Sea Breeze. The sailboat’s fuel had been contaminated with water; that mast was beyond repair, and the vessel no longer seaworthy.The Navy considered towing the sailboat but decided it was impossible. Pham eventually gave permission for the crew to sink it. He went below deck while sailors used smoke floats to set the Sea Breeze alight. He could, however, not bear to watch. After all, the boat had also been his home.A survivor’s past and the journey back homePham had arrived in the United States from Vietnam in 1976 as a refugee, the Los Angeles Times reported. He had owned furniture shops in North Hollywood, Culver City and Los Angeles, alongside an auto repair business. Unfortunately, a decade before his voyage, a car accident left him in a coma for six months. Consequently, he suffered serious memory loss and had to relearn English along with everyday tasks. Unable to run his business, he spent his savings on hospital bills.By 2002, he was retired and living aboard the Sea Breeze, which he kept in Long Beach between trips. Before it sank, he had managed to retrieve his green card. However, he had no permanent lodging in Long Beach and had left behind an apartment in downtown Los Angeles, the Los Angeles Times reported. USS McClusky took Pham to Puerto Quetzal, Guatemala, and, as the Los Angeles Times reported, the sailors raised $800 for his plane fare.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Who is El Chapo Isidro, the alleged cartel boss arrested in Mexico?
articles.summary: Mexican forces arrested Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa. He was on the FBI’s most wanted list and faces US drug charges.
articles.body:
Mexican special forces have arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “Chapo Isidro”, who is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, Mexico’s defence ministry said.

Meza-Flores was detained along with two other men on Friday night in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa.

The arrest comes as US President Donald Trump has been pressing Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to do more to combat drug cartels and said on Friday that Washington was working with Sheinbaum “because the cartels are running Mexico.”

“I told her that,” he said. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbour.”

Who is Chapo Isidro and what is he accused of?

Despite the similar nickname, Meza-Flores is not related to Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman, the jailed former leader of the Sinaloa Cartel.

Mexican authorities say Meza-Flores leads the Beltran Leyva criminal organisation and is an ally of the Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. The Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said he was wanted in Mexico on an arrest warrant for organised crime and drug offences and is subject to an extradition order to the United States.

US prosecutors first indicted Meza-Flores in 2012. In a 2019 indictment, they accused him of conspiring to manufacture and distribute cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana for the US market between 2005 and 2019. He also faces a firearms charge.

The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025, and the US Department of State offered up to $5m for information leading to his arrest and conviction.

“Known as El Chapo Isidro, he’s accused of spending the last 20 years flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and other deadly drugs, first as an independent drug trafficker and later as the head of the Meza-Flores cartel,” said then-acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll in announcing his addition to the list.

He also said Meza-Flores and his organisation were accused of kidnapping, extortion, torture and murder.

Mexico’s defence ministry said the operation followed coordination between Mexican and US intelligence agencies and involved special forces from Mexico’s National Guard and army.

Troops used “stealth and surprise” to establish a security perimeter around a house in Guasave and came under attack with gunfire and explosives before entering and arresting three men, the ministry said.

It identified the other two as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, who they identified as a financial operator. The three men were flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.

Sinaloa’s public security agency urged residents to stay indoors, avoid the area, and stay off the roads, as federal personnel had been attacked in Guasave.

The defence ministry said roadblocks were reported in four areas of Sinaloa after the arrests and that security forces were sent to reopen roads.

Videos from Guasave showed people fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as cars and petrol stations on fire, The Associated Press news agency reported.

Mexico’s security secretary, Omar Garcia Harfuch, said on Saturday that troops would remain in Sinaloa to protect residents.

“These detentions are an important step toward restoring peace in Sinaloa,” he wrote on X.
