articles.title: California school board defies state by passing policy banning trans athletes from girls sports
articles.summary: Chino Valley Unified approved a policy barring biological males from girls sports, locker rooms and showers, defying a warning from Rob Bonta's office.
articles.body: A California school district has adopted a sweeping new policy barring biological males from girls sports, locker rooms and showers, setting up a potential legal showdown with state officials who warned the district against approving the restrictions. The Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education voted 4-1 Thursday to approve the policy authored by outgoing board President Sonja Shaw, despite opposition from California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office and the district's teachers union. Shaw, who has previously clashed with California officials over parental rights and transgender student policies, said the vote marked a significant escalation in her efforts to protect female athletes and called on other school districts across the state to follow. MICHIGAN SCHOOL BOARD VOTES TO BAN BIOLOGICAL MALES FROM GIRLS' SPORTS IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT "Yesterday we passed a policy I authored that went beyond statements and resolutions," Shaw told OutKick on Friday. "Last night we took it further. We passed actual board policy that establishes clear protections for girls in sports, locker rooms, showers, and overnight school travel." "These are common-sense measures: no boys competing in girls’ sports, no boys sharing girls’ locker rooms or showers, and no boys and girls sharing hotel rooms on school trips. They protect girls’ privacy and safety in the most basic ways." Shaw claimed Chino Valley Unified is the first California school district to formally adopt such restrictions, following a resolution she authored in 2025 that was subsequently adopted by other districts. "We are the first district in California to put these protections into formal board policy," she said. "We have millions of children in public schools across this state, and parents should not have to wonder whether their daughters’ privacy and safety are being protected." The policy, titled "Fairness in Girls' Athletics and Privacy in Sex-Based Facilities," establishes eligibility for girls athletic teams based on biological sex at birth rather than gender identity. Under the accompanying administrative regulations, eligibility will generally be determined using existing student enrollment records reflecting sex at or near birth. When those records are unavailable or have been amended, the district may require a birth certificate issued around the time of birth or a statement from a licensed healthcare provider based on a routine athletic physical. The regulations also explicitly prohibit requiring students to undergo additional examinations, tests or inspections beyond the standard physical required of all athletes. Shaw said the changes go beyond symbolic opposition to California's existing transgender student policies. "I authored the original resolution because someone needed to stand up and say enough. Yesterday I took that fight to the next level and gratefully our board passed it with a majority," she said. "I am sick and tired of adults pointing fingers about who is responsible and who can fix it. More districts should follow." "The only controversy here should be that there was any opposition at all." FEDERAL JUDGE DISMISSES DOJ LAWSUIT CHALLENGING CALIFORNIA POLICY ALLOWING BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS’ SPORTS The vote came one day after Bonta's office sent the district a letter warning that the proposed restrictions conflicted with California law. Deputy Attorney General Edward Nugent urged the district to reject or postpone the policy. "Because the Proposed Policies conflict with Education Code ... the Board should reject the proposal, or at the very least, delay the vote to allow for discussion of the District’s understanding regarding the applicability of state law to the Proposed Policies," Nugent wrote in a Wednesday letter to the school system. The law, enacted through Assembly Bill 1266 in 2013, has been a central point of conflict between California officials and the Trump administration over transgender participation in girls sports. Shaw rejected the state's warning and publicly challenged Bonta, arguing that federal law takes precedence over conflicting state requirements. The district's policy specifically invokes the U.S. Supreme Court's June 30 decision in West Virginia v. B.P.J. and Little v. Hecox , which upheld laws in West Virginia and Idaho restricting participation in female sports to biological females. However that ruling only protects the state laws that currently exist to protect women's sports. In California, the state continues to maintain laws allowing transgender students to compete according to their gender identity. In August, a federal district court dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against the California Department of Education and CIF over the state's transgender athlete policies. The court did not resolve the broader question of whether transgender participation in girls sports violates Title IX, instead finding insufficient legal notice to justify imposing the federal government's interpretation as a condition of funding. The Chino Valley policy directs the superintendent to consult legal counsel and take lawful steps to protect students and federal funding if state requirements are applied in a manner that conflicts with the district's new restrictions. The vote came during Shaw's final meeting on the Chino Valley school board after she unsuccessfully ran for California superintendent of public instruction earlier this month. Shaw has emerged as one of California's most outspoken school board officials on parental rights and transgender student policies, previously leading efforts to require schools to notify parents about certain changes in their children's gender identification. That policy became the subject of litigation involving Bonta's office, part of an ongoing dispute over parental notification requirements and state protections for transgender students. In her latest statement, Shaw directly challenged California's political and educational leadership, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, Bonta, lawmakers, teachers unions and the California Department of Education. articles.title: Former GOP staffer indicted over fake anti-Trump attack, allegedly paid to have face cut and zip-tied herself
articles.summary: Two New Jersey women were indicted after being accused of falsely reporting that one of them, a former staffer for U.S.
articles.body: Two New Jersey women were indicted after being accused of falsely reporting that one of them, a former staffer for U.S. Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., was the target of a violent political attack in 2025. On Friday, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Jersey announced that Natalie Greene, 27, of Ocean City, was indicted on charges of conspiracy to convey false statements and hoaxes, conveying false statements and hoaxes, and making false statements to federal law enforcement. She had previously been charged with the same offenses in a federal criminal complaint. Officials said Anamaria Moe, 25, of Atlantic City, was newly charged in the indictment with conspiracy to convey false statements and hoaxes and conveying false statements and hoaxes. Moe made her initial appearance in federal court in Camden on Thursday. On July 23, 2025, prosecutors said Moe called 911 and claimed she and Greene had been attacked by three men while walking on a trail at a nature preserve in Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey. Officials said Moe told authorities that the men called Greene by name and referenced her employment with a federal official, later identified as Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew. When police arrived at the scene, they found Greene on the ground in a wooded area near the trail with her hands and feet bound with black zip ties. Greene’s shirt was pulled over her head and secured with a zip tie, investigators said. Greene also had several lacerations on her face, neck, upper chest and shoulder, according to officials. Police said the words “TRUMP WHORE” were written on her stomach, while a message claiming that Van Drew “IS RACIST” was written on her back. Greene told police that at least one of the men who allegedly attacked her said he had a gun and threatened to shoot her, investigators said. She also claimed that at least one of the alleged attackers held her down, restrained her, cut her and wrote on her body. Greene received medical treatment for her lacerations and repeated her account of the supposed attack to law enforcement officers, including an FBI agent, a few days later. During the investigation, however, officials determined Greene had lied about the attack. Instead, Greene paid a body modification/scarification artist to cut the lacerations on her face, neck, chest and shoulder based on a design that she provided, according to investigators. Police also recovered black zip ties from Greene’s car on the night of the alleged attack which were similar to the zip ties that had been used to bind her arms and feet, officials said. Investigators also said that two days before the alleged attack, Moe’s cellphone had been used to search “zip ties near me.” Van Drew spoke about the allegations back in 2025. “I’m just praying for her,” he said. “Wish her the very best. I don’t know anything more than you all do and we never would interfere with an investigation.” In a 2025 statement, Greene’s lawyer, Louis Barbone, said in part that she served her community with “loyalty and fidelity” while working for Van Drew and that under the law, “she is presumed innocent.” Each of the charged counts has a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment, a $250,000 fine and a term of three years of supervised release.

articles.title: Russian strike kills two, wounds 60, in Zelenskyy’s hometown
articles.summary: Attack on Kryvyi Rih comes as Russian missiles land in NATO member Poland and US-led peace efforts face uncertainty.
articles.body:
A Russian attack on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown of Kryvyi Rih has killed two people and wounded 60 others, according to local officials.

The strikes hit the central Ukrainian city on Friday night, killing a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while six children were among the injured.

About 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and businesses were damaged, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s city administration.

Vilkul said on Saturday that Russian forces launched further missiles after emergency workers arrived, hitting rescuers, medical personnel and utility crews.

Footage released by Ukraine’s emergency services appeared to show additional strikes during the rescue operation.

Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine killed two people in the southern Zaporizhia region, according to its governor.

Russian authorities also reported six deaths, including a child, from a Ukrainian attack on a residential area in Russian-controlled Luhansk, an eastern Ukrainian region.

The violence followed a separate incident on Friday in which two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in southeastern Poland, a member of NATO, the military alliance linking the United States, Canada and European countries.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident on Friday as a deliberate provocation, questioning its timing alongside military exercises involving European countries preparing for a possible post-war security mission in Ukraine.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte condemned the airspace violation on Saturday and pledged that the alliance would defend Polish territory.

The incidents have unfolded as US President Donald Trump seeks progress in negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv.

Trump said on Friday, following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China, that the Russian leader wanted to end the war diplomatically.

Zelenskyy, however, told reporters in Kyiv on Saturday that he remained less convinced than Washington that Putin was prepared to compromise.

Moscow continues to demand Ukrainian withdrawal from the entire eastern Donbas region, which Kyiv refuses to surrender.

Zelenskyy also reaffirmed Ukraine’s ambition to join NATO, while Washington has discussed offering Kyiv security guarantees resembling the alliance’s collective-defence commitments.

Such guarantees remain under discussion as negotiations continue over how to end the war and protect Ukraine from future attacks.

articles.title: Actor Michael Sheen and other Welsh celebrities backed a children's hospice appeal inspired by a family who lost their five-year-old son; it raised £264,695 in 56 hours, beating a £200,000 target
articles.summary: A Welsh children’s hospice has raised £264,695 in 56 hours, beating its £200,000 target for the Every Precious Life appeal.
articles.body: A Welsh children’s hospice has raised £264,695 in 56 hours, beating its £200,000 target for the Every Precious Life appeal. The campaign was inspired by William Watkins, a five year old boy from Cowbridge who received care at Tŷ Hafan before he died in 2021, according to Business in Wales and Charity News Desk.Actor Michael Sheen and other Welsh celebrities backed the appeal by sharing William’s story on social media. The money will help Tŷ Hafan expand its support for children with life shortening conditions and their families.How the appeal workedThe Every Precious Life appeal ran from 10am on Monday 16 November to 6pm on Wednesday 18 November. It was a match funding campaign, meaning every pound donated was worth twice as much thanks to a team of match funders.The goal was to raise £200,000. The hospice reached that target just before 10am on Wednesday, then continued to bring in donations until the appeal closed. The final total was £264,695. The amount reflects the combined impact of public donations and the match funding arrangement.Why William’s story matteredWilliam Watkins was diagnosed with cancer at the age of three. He spent the final weeks of his life at Tŷ Hafan’s hospice near Sully with his parents, Nicola and Ian. William died on 1 May 2021, shortly after his fifth birthday. His parents chose to share his story as part of the appeal to help other families in similar situations.Nicola said she and Ian were proud that William’s story helped raise essential funds. She thanked everyone involved in the campaign and everyone who donated.Who backed the appealTŷ Hafan’s celebrity supporters included Michael Sheen, Ruth Jones, Leigh Halfpenny and his wife Jess, Nigel Owens, and former Traitors star Andrew Jenkins. They shared William’s story on their social media feeds throughout the appeal window.Their support helped bring attention to the campaign. It also gave the appeal a wider reach beyond the hospice’s usual network of donors.The involvement of well known figures gave the campaign a sense of momentum. It helped turn a local story into a broader effort to raise money for children’s hospice care.What the money will doTŷ Hafan is one of only two children’s hospices in Wales. It provides specialist palliative care that addresses the physical, emotional, social, and spiritual needs of each family member.The hospice currently supports around 300 children with life shortening conditions and around 3,000 family members each year. More than 80 percent of its funding comes from public donations.The Every Precious Life appeal is designed to expand services. The money raised will help Tŷ Hafan support more families through life, death, and beyond.What comes nextThe hospice says it can currently reach around one in 10 families with a child who could benefit from its support. The new funds will help close that gap.Dan Bamsey, head of fundraising at Tŷ Hafan, said the response was beyond what the organisation expected. He thanked donors for their generosity and said their support means the world to the hospice.The appeal’s success shows how a personal story, combined with community support and celebrity backing, can turn into a major fundraising effort. For William’s family, it is a way to keep his memory alive while helping others.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Mike Waltz warns Kremlin faces 'unsustainable' losses approaching WWII scale as Trump seeks deal
articles.summary: United Nations Ambassador Mike Waltz says Russia is losing up to 35,000 troops a month in Ukraine, calling the battlefield losses "unsustainable."
articles.body: U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz warned Friday that Russia is suffering "unsustainable" battlefield losses, with monthly deaths outpacing recruitment numbers. Speaking on "The Brian Kilmeade Show" podcast, Waltz echoed President Donald Trump's assessment that Russian President Vladimir Putin is "worn down," arguing the war in Ukraine cannot be won militarily and must end at the negotiating table. "Right now, the numbers that we have, the Russians are recruiting 20,000 to 25,000 a month of new fresh recruits," Waltz said. "They're losing 30,000 to 35,000 a month, dead every single month." TRUMP CLAIMS STUNNING CASUALTY NUMBERS IN RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR "That is exponentially more than they lost in Afghanistan and approaching what they lost in World War II, a thousand a day," he added. "It's just unsustainable." The interview followed Trump's return from Shenzhen, China, where he met with Putin before joining the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping for the first-ever three-way summit between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China. CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO The summit produced a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, maintaining stable energy supplies and reforming the United Nations, but the leaders stopped short of announcing breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran. At a White House news conference Friday, Trump addressed questions about Putin's intent regarding the war. ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH "He'd love to end the war. It's a very hard thing to do," Trump said Friday. "To be honest, you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them." "You have two people that hate each other, Zelenskyy and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it," he added. "And it's a horrible war, actually. And I thought it would have been maybe one of the easier ones to get ended. But the personalities play." KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION Waltz argued that both Ukraine and Russia have "worn each other down," saying it's unlikely the two countries will be able to sustain the current level of fighting. "It's a horrific war, and the president remains determined to find some construct of a deal that will end it because neither side can sustain this war of attrition," Waltz said. "There is no winning it militarily. It's got to end diplomatically." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital’s Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

articles.title: FBI national crime database suffers suspected breach: Reports
articles.summary: The reported hacking is the latest in a string of breaches and outages affecting the US government.
articles.body:
The FBI’s national criminal database has suffered a suspected breach, according to multiple US media reports.

President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly downplayed breaches affecting departments within his administration, appeared to confirm the FBI hacking during a television interview on Saturday.

“Well, we just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that,” Trump told Fox News.

On Friday, CNN and NBC reported that the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which is used by law enforcement agencies across the United States to share information on criminal warrants and background checks, was compromised, citing two people who had been briefed on the matter.

The reported hacking, which would be the second to hit the bureau this year, is the latest in a string of US government breaches and outages that have alarmed officials over the past week.

In a separate incident, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture.

The FBI and USDA did not immediately return Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

In the interview on Saturday, Trump suggested the hack of the FBI’s crucial database could be viewed with “a positive spin”.

“Maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise. You had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. You had all these other hoaxes,” he said in an apparent reference to his discontent with the FBI’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 US election.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber group that claimed it had stolen sensitive information on the bureau’s 38,000 employees.

Additionally, in March, the agency said it had been investigating “suspicious activities” on some of its internal systems, The Associated Press news agency reported.

FBI Director Kash Patel, who has not publicly commented on the most recent hacking, was not present for a Wednesday hearing at the US Capitol to examine threats against the US. Patel’s deputy, Christopher Raia, attended in his place, joining US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

articles.title: An Indiana man bought a condo hoping to live with his daughter, but missed homeowners' fees and faced a $9,213 judgment; even after paying $9,489, an appeals court ruled he still owed more
articles.summary: An Indiana man who bought a condominium hoping to move in with his daughter has lost an appeal over unpaid homeowners' association fees, after a court
articles.body: An Indiana man who bought a condominium hoping to move in with his daughter has lost an appeal over unpaid homeowners' association fees, after a court upheld a judgment against him and remanded the case for the determination of the association's reasonable appellate attorneys' fees. Onnie James Florence Jr. purchased a unit at Meridian Arch Condominiums in 2020 but continued living in Illinois because he was unable to move into the property. After he fell behind on monthly assessments, the homeowners' association obtained a $9,213.50 default judgment against him in 2021. Florence later paid $9,489, but the association pursued additional unpaid assessments, late fees and legal expenses. In a November 19, 2026 memorandum decision, available on Justia, the Indiana Court of Appeals affirmed the subsequent summary judgment in favour of the association and sent the case back to the trial court to determine its appellate attorneys' fees.Condo purchase led to unpaid association assessmentsFlorence bought the condominium at Meridian Arch Condominiums in 2020, intending to live there with his daughter. However, he was unable to make the move and continued residing at his home in Illinois. Although he did not occupy the Indiana property, Florence remained responsible for paying its monthly homeowners' association assessments. Under the association's rules, unpaid assessments could become a lien against the condominium and eventually lead to foreclosure.By May 2021, Florence owed $5,229.80 in unpaid assessments. The Meridian Arch Owners Association filed a lawsuit seeking to foreclose on its lien. The association initially attempted to serve Florence personally but was unsuccessful. It then sent the summons and complaint by certified mail to his Illinois residence. His wife signed for the documents on June 15, 2021.Florence did not respond to the lawsuit or appear in court. The association subsequently requested a default judgment, submitting an affidavit showing that he owed $9,213.50 as of September 14, 2021. The amount included unpaid assessments, late fees, collection costs and attorneys' fees. The trial court granted the request on September 28, 2021.Florence challenged the judgment and paid $9,489After the association began proceedings to sell the condominium through a sheriff's sale, Florence appeared in the case and asked the court to set aside the default judgment. He argued that he had not received the necessary court filings and that the association had filed its foreclosure complaint prematurely. He also sought dismissal of the case, arguing that the association had failed to notify CrossCountry Mortgage, the holder of the property's first mortgage, before initiating the proceedings. The trial court rejected both requests in January 2024.In April 2024, a foreclosure decree was sent to the sheriff for the sale of the condominium. However, the sale was cancelled after Florence paid the association $9,489. The association treated the payment as a partial satisfaction of the existing judgment because post-judgment interest had accumulated. It later informed the court that Florence still owed $1,922.84 on the original judgment's principal portion because of accrued interest. The association also sought to recover additional assessments, late fees, costs and attorneys' fees that had accumulated after the original judgment.Association pursued additional unpaid feesIn November 2024, the association obtained permission to set aside the original default judgment and amend its complaint to include the additional amounts that had accrued since the initial case was filed. Its amended complaint sought recovery of the outstanding assessments and related expenses. CrossCountry Mortgage was also joined as a party.In September 2025, the association requested summary judgment, submitting evidence that Florence owed $26,813.22 in unpaid assessments, late fees, costs and attorneys' fees. Its affidavit specifically recorded that his $9,489 payment had been credited to his account on August 20, 2024. Florence received two extensions to respond to the summary-judgment request but did not file a response. The trial court granted the association's motion on February 3, 2026.Florence subsequently challenged the decision, arguing that the association had failed to account properly for his payment and that he should have received a detailed accounting of how the money was applied.Appeals court upholds judgment and orders determination of legal feesThe Indiana Court of Appeals examined Florence's arguments and found no basis to overturn the trial court's decision. The judges noted that Florence's wife had signed for the original complaint and summons sent to his Illinois residence, satisfying the state's service requirements. They also found that his challenge to the denial of his request to set aside the original default judgment had been filed too late for appellate review.Regarding the $9,489 payment, the court pointed to the association's affidavit, which explicitly confirmed that the amount had been credited to Florence's account. He had not submitted evidence contradicting that record or showing that the payment had been omitted from the calculations. The court also rejected his argument that the association had failed to include the mortgage lender, noting that CrossCountry had subsequently been added to the amended proceedings.In its November 19, 2026 decision, the appeals court affirmed the summary judgment in favour of the Meridian Arch Owners Association and remanded the case to the trial court to determine reasonable appellate attorneys' fees owed to the association. The decision was issued as a memorandum decision under Indiana Appellate Rule 65(D), meaning it is not binding precedent for other courts and may be cited only for persuasive purposes or certain limited legal proceedings. Florence's $9,489 payment therefore did not eliminate his outstanding obligations. The association's judgment remained in place, with the additional appellate legal fees still to be determined.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Why is the US Army detonating lead-rich explosives in Iowa?
articles.summary: The delayed blasts have stoked environmental fears and concerns about health effects in the state.
articles.body:
The United States Army is slated to conduct two controlled detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the Midwestern state of Iowa, aiming to destroy 68 drums of degraded lead azide — a highly volatile, lead-based explosive used to trigger the main charges in some conventional munitions.

Announced just five days before an original Friday, November 20, detonation date, the Army’s decision was authorised by an emergency permit issued by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

Residents, environmental health experts, and Iowa elected officials have decried the detonation of lead-rich explosive material, citing scant public notice and potential environmental and health harms.

In a statement posted on X on Thursday, Iowa Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek stressed the need for greater transparency.

“Iowans deserve to know that every safety precaution has been taken and exactly what the associated health risks are. Until those questions are answered, the detonation should not proceed,” he wrote.

Mounting public pressure has prompted the military to push the controlled blasts back to Monday, November 23.

But a late-stage legal challenge has cast doubt on whether the army will be able to proceed at all.

On the eve of the originally scheduled operation, two Iowa environmental advocacy groups — the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter — petitioned a federal appeals court to overturn the EPA emergency permit, arguing that the agency had not given the public meaningful advance notice, failed to require adequate safeguards to protect human health and the environment, and sanctioned the operation without sufficient consideration of safer disposal alternatives.

What is happening at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant?

In a November 15 advisory , the US Army warned residents of Middletown, a southeastern Iowa city of about 360 people, that the emergency blasts would loft a dust plume containing “some lead”, accompanied by loud explosions and ground vibrations.

The army’s containment strategy centres on thoroughly drenching the soil above the existing igloo-like, earth-covered concrete magazines — where the chemicals have been stored — with water before and during the detonations to help suppress airborne dust and particles.

The magazines are ringed by sand-filled barriers rising roughly two storeys high, designed to eject the force of the blast vertically into the sky, rather than laterally across the surrounding landscape.

“These measures should reduce the amount of lead that migrates from the detonation through the air off the installation,” the advisory reads.

According to the military’s modelling predictions, the blasts will deliver elevated airborne lead levels, but will remain “below the level at which EPA would require protective actions be taken”.

That’s reassurance with a blind spot, experts say.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy, an environmental health professor at the University of Iowa, who will be monitoring the environmental fallout from the detonations, says that for all the assumed precision of the army’s modelling, its most consequential variable remains undisclosed to the public: precisely how much lead each explosion will propel into the air.

It is the very quantity that will shape the scale of the downwind exposure.

“The unprecedented aspect of it is that normally in the world of air pollution, we have some estimation of what’s called the emission factor, the emission strength. We know how many pounds per second will be distributed out into the air from a smokestack,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera, “but in this case, we have no idea.”

The longer-term, more invisible peril, O’Shaughnessy said, is lead settling on playground equipment, getting into crops, landing in back yards and on other play surfaces where people could be exposed.

Why is the US Army detonating the explosives?

During a safety review in March, technicians discovered a stockpile of deteriorating lead azide that had languished in storage bunkers for 20 years at its Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a sprawling 19,000-acre installation in Des Moines County, about 16 kilometres (10 miles) west of the Mississippi River, which separates Iowa and the state of Illinois.

Since then, the Army says it has engaged with the local community, including at an open house at the Army Reserve Center in mid-October for residents within a 50-mile (80km) radius of the facility, where it outlined its developing plans to eliminate the explosive hazard.

The stockpile includes roughly 9,700 pounds (just under five tonnes) of the explosives across 68 barrels, set to be detonated in place — material that contains roughly 6,900 pounds (about 3.5 tonnes) of lead by chemical mass.

During long-term storage, liquid in the drums evaporated and caused the lead azide to recrystallise.

According to the environmental assessment for Lead Azide Risk Mitigation, prepared by the Army, the recrystallisation had heightened the material’s sensitivity to shock and friction.

“Due to its chemical degradation, the material’s legal status transitioned from a viable production component to an unserviceable hazardous waste,” the report states.

Army Sustainment Command spokesperson Justine Barati said the Army faced a narrowing window to destroy the chemical material before colder weather or disturbances increased the risk of spontaneous detonation, which would pose an unacceptable risk of killing technicians on-site.

“We’re trying to do a controlled detonation to minimise the impact to the community and the environment. This is not something that we take lightly. We know that this is a disruption to people and that is not our intent, but we’re trying to do this in the safest manner possible,” Barati told a local television news station earlier this week.

Elemental lead cannot be destroyed by heat. It decomposes, melts, vaporises or fragments into fine particulate dust.

“Everyone should be shocked to learn this problem has been left long enough to warrant the potential catastrophic fallout from this situation,” said Dr Aaron Specht, an associate professor at Purdue University’s School of Health Sciences.

A fact sheet issued by the Army in advance of the scheduled disposal asserts that the heat generated by a proper detonation “incinerates” the lead azide.

Bruce Lanphear, a paediatric epidemiologist and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University, disputed the chemistry explanation.

“When lead azide detonates, it decomposes primarily into nitrogen gas and lead,” he told Al Jazeera, “the lead may be released as fine particles of metallic lead, lead oxides, and other lead compounds. The explosion doesn’t destroy the lead. It redistributes it.”

The risks of lead exposure are particularly pronounced for fetuses exposed in utero through the mother’s bloodstream, as well as the pregnant women themselves. Young children, whose developing nervous systems are acutely susceptible to lead, are also at risk. Because of their smaller body mass, comparatively little lead is required to reach biologically significant doses in children.

Lead can cause serious harm even below regulatory limits.

There is no blood level of lead in a child that is deemed safe, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Lanphear has spent four decades studying how even low-level lead exposure can severely blunt children’s cognitive function.

“The danger of lead exposure as a distinct threat has been known for over a hundred years,” said Lanphear, “the neurotoxin causes permanent neuropsychological and developmental injuries … lower IQ, less tolerance for frustration, ADHD, and weak executive control functions.”

At high doses, lead poisoning can precipitate encephalopathy, a severe disturbance of brain function, or induce premature death.

Lead also figures prominently in cardiovascular mortality, said Lanphear, who co-authored a 2018 study estimating that long-term lead exposure was linked to 412,000 deaths annually across the US, including 256,000 deaths from cardiovascular disease.

While the original detonation was scheduled for Friday, Army acting Secretary Adam R Telle announced on social media Thursday night that the operation would be postponed until Monday, which he described as “the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material”.

The Army did not announce a time for the deferred blasts.

Later on Thursday, in response to the Iowa groups’ lawsuit, the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted an interim stay of the EPA’s emergency authorisation, temporarily blocking the military from proceeding while the court weighed the groups’ request for a longer-term injunction.

It is an interim measure, not a final ruling on the legality of the permit.

The Army cannot technically detonate the chemicals under its EPA permit while the suspension remains in force, but the court may lift the pause beforehand.

While the court has put the brakes on the planned detonation for now, Justice Department lawyers, on Friday, pointed to separate emergency powers that the federal government could still invoke to bypass the permit requirement and press ahead with the blasts.
